Bateman equations used

For each radioactive nuclide \(i\):
\[\frac{dN_i}{dt}=-\lambda_i N_i+\sum_j b_{j\to i}\lambda_jN_j\] \[\lambda_i=\frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}},\qquad A_i(t)=\lambda_iN_i(t).\]
The simulator evaluates the coupled linear Bateman decay network using the measured half-lives and branching fractions in the embedded dataset. Stable daughters have \(\lambda=0\) and accumulate as terminal populations.

MASS & BINDING

Experimental B is reconstructed from the NUBASE2020 atomic mass excess. The shell-correction curve is defined here as the empirical residual Bexp − BSEMF; it is not a microscopic Strutinsky shell correction.

Selected calculation

Hover a point to inspect the nucleus.

Equations

Binding energy
$$B = Z\Delta_H + N\Delta_n - \Delta(A,Z)$$
Binding energy per nucleon
$$B/A = \frac{B}{A}$$
SEMF / liquid-drop model
$$B_{\rm SEMF}=a_vA-a_sA^{2/3}-a_c\frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{1/3}}-a_a\frac{(A-2Z)^2}{A}+\delta$$
Pairing
$$\delta=\begin{cases}+a_pA^{-1/2},&ee\\0,&odd\ A\\-a_pA^{-1/2},&oo\end{cases}$$
Shell correction used in explorer
$$\Delta B_{\rm shell}^{\rm(emp)}=B_{\rm exp}-B_{\rm SEMF}$$
Neutron separation
$$S_n=B(A,Z)-B(A-1,Z)$$
Proton separation
$$S_p=B(A,Z)-B(A-1,Z-1)$$
Two-nucleon separation
$$S_{2n}=B(A,Z)-B(A-2,Z),\quad S_{2p}=B(A,Z)-B(A-2,Z-2)$$
Mass-excess form: Sₙ = Δ(A−1,Z)+Δₙ−Δ(A,Z), Sₚ = Δ(A−1,Z−1)+Δ_H−Δ(A,Z). All plotted energies are in MeV.

DRIP-LINE DETECTOR

Neutron/proton drip-line candidates are identified from the sign of the one-nucleon separation energy: Sₙ ≤ 0 or Sₚ ≤ 0. The detector reports the boundary candidates present in the NUBASE2020 ground-state set.

DETECTOR SUMMARY

Equations & criteria

Neutron separation
$$S_n=B(A,Z)-B(A-1,Z)$$
Proton separation
$$S_p=B(A,Z)-B(A-1,Z-1)$$
Neutron drip line
$$S_n\le0\;\Rightarrow\; ext{neutron-unbound candidate}$$
Proton drip line
$$S_p\le0\;\Rightarrow\; ext{proton-unbound candidate}$$
Two-neutron shell gap
$$\Delta_{2n}(N,Z)=S_{2n}(N,Z)-S_{2n}(N+2,Z)$$
Two-proton shell gap
$$\Delta_{2p}(Z,N)=S_{2p}(Z,N)-S_{2p}(Z+2,N)$$
Magic-number candidates
$$\Delta_{2n},\Delta_{2p}\; ext{large}\;\Rightarrow\; ext{shell-closure candidate}$$
Reference magic numbers
$$2,\;8,\;20,\;28,\;50,\;82,\;126$$
The shell detector uses the local two-particle separation-energy discontinuity. A large positive gap is a shell-closure signal; the threshold is user-adjustable. It is a diagnostic, not a microscopic shell-model calculation.

UNIVERSAL FIT RANKING (0 candidates)
Parameter key: A = mass number (nucleons, N+Z) · Z = proton number of the parent nuclide · N = neutron number of the parent (A−Z) · Z_d = daughter proton number after α emission (Z−2) · Qα = alpha-decay Q-value (MeV, energy released) · Ã = reduced mass number of the emitted α + daughter system, Ã = A₁·A₂/(A₁+A₂) with A₁=4 (α particle) and A₂=A−4 (daughter) · χ, ρ = the two variables of the Universal Decay Law (Qi–Xu–Liotta–Wyss, 2009): χ = Z·Z_d·√(Ã/Qα), ρ = √(Ã·Z·Z_d·(A₁¹ᐟ³+A₂¹ᐟ³)); together they give the best two-parameter fit to log T in the original UDL paper · logT₁₀ = log₁₀ of the half-life T₁/₂ in seconds (the fitted quantity). Each candidate term above is one function of these built from the parent nuclide's data; a0, a1, a2… are the fitted slope(s) for that term and b0, b1, b2… the fitted intercepts, found by ordinary least-squares regression of logT₁₀ against the term(s) for the currently filtered set of α-emitters.

CORRELATION ANALYSIS — log₁₀T₁/₂ vs. each parameter

Pearson correlation coefficient r between log₁₀T₁/₂ and each candidate quantity, computed over the currently filtered α-emitter set. Correlation is computed against log₁₀T₁/₂ (not T itself) because half-lives span ~30 orders of magnitude and a linear correlation on the raw values would be dominated entirely by the most extreme outliers. Significance uses a two-tailed t-test on r (H₀: no linear correlation), with n−2 degrees of freedom.
Parameterrr²ntp (two-tailed)Significant (p<0.05)

BAYESIAN LINEAR REGRESSION

Conjugate Normal-Inverse-Gamma Bayesian regression of log₁₀T₁/₂ on a single chosen parameter x (weakly-informative prior: coefficient precision λ=10⁻⁶, variance prior a₀=b₀=10⁻³). This gives full posterior distributions for the slope and intercept instead of single point estimates, plus a Bayes factor comparing "x predicts log T" against the null model (intercept only, i.e. x has no effect).

Reference · NUBASE2020 Decay Systematics

Decay theory, equations and numerical methods

01Decay energetics and the Q value

The explorer uses the embedded NUBASE2020 atomic mass-excess dataset. For alpha decay, the stored \(Q_\alpha\) value is converted from keV to MeV before fitting and plotting.

$$Q_\alpha=(M_p-M_d-M_\alpha)c^2,\qquad Q_\alpha>0\Rightarrow\text{energetically allowed }\alpha\text{ decay}.$$
Parameters: \(Q_\alpha\) = alpha-decay energy (MeV); \(M_p\) = parent atomic mass; \(M_d\) = daughter atomic mass; \(M_\alpha\) = alpha-particle mass; \(c\) = speed of light. Meaning: \(Q_\alpha\) is the energy released by the decay. \(Q_\alpha>0\) means alpha decay is energetically allowed. The explorer uses the tabulated NUBASE2020 \(Q_\alpha\), not a fitted mass formula.

02βBeta-minus and beta-plus decay

Beta decay is a weak-interaction process, not a barrier-tunnelling problem. The explorer does not solve the full Fermi theory for each decay channel. Instead, it uses the tabulated NUBASE2020 decay energies \(Q_{\beta^-}\) and \(Q_{\beta^+}\), then fits empirical systematics in \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\) space.

$$\beta^-: n\to p+e^-+\bar{\nu}_e,\qquad Q_{\beta^-}=\big[M(A,Z)-M(A,Z+1)\big]c^2,$$ $$\beta^+: p\to n+e^+ + \nu_e,\qquad Q_{\beta^+}=\big[M(A,Z)-M(A,Z-1)-2m_e c^2\big]c^2,$$ $$\lambda_\beta = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} \propto \int_0^{Q_\beta} p_eE_e(Q_\beta-E_e)^2 F(Z,E_e)\,|M_F|^2\,dE_e.$$
Parameters: \(Q_{\beta^-}\), \(Q_{\beta^+}\) = the energy released in beta-minus or beta-plus decay; \(M(A,Z)\) = atomic mass of the nuclide; \(m_e\) = electron rest mass; \(p_e,E_e\) = emitted lepton momentum and total energy; \(F(Z,E_e)\) = Fermi function; \(|M_F|\) = nuclear matrix element. Meaning: a positive \(Q\) means the decay is energetically allowed. The phase-space part grows rapidly with \(Q\), but the decay rate also depends strongly on the nuclear matrix element and on selection rules such as allowed/forbidden transitions. In this explorer, the numerical input is the tabulated NUBASE2020 Q value; the code does not evaluate the full weak-interaction integral for each decay.
Empirical beta systematics: for allowed beta transitions one often uses the Sargent-rule trend \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\approx a+b/\sqrt{Q_\beta}\). The viewer’s \(\beta^-\) and \(\beta^+/\mathrm{EC}\) fits follow the same philosophy: use the measured or tabulated Q value as the dominant energetic variable and fit the logarithm of the half-life. This is a compact summary of weak-decay systematics, not a microscopic calculation of the weak matrix element.

02Geiger–Nuttall systematics

The basic alpha relation is fitted in \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\) space with ordinary least squares. The implementation has two fitted coefficients.

$$\boxed{\log_{10}T_{1/2}=\frac{a}{\sqrt{Q_\alpha}}+b}$$
Parameters: \(T_{1/2}\) = experimental or predicted half-life; \(Q_\alpha\) = alpha-decay energy (MeV); \(a\) = fitted coefficient controlling the dependence on \(1/\sqrt{Q_\alpha}\); \(b\) = fitted intercept. Units: \(a\) has units of MeV\(^{1/2}\) when \(Q\) is in MeV; \(b\) is dimensionless because it is added to \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\). Meaning: increasing \(Q_\alpha\) normally decreases the predicted half-life.

03Viola–Seaborg-type alpha relation

The richer alpha fit adds proton-number dependence and odd-\(Z\)/odd-\(N\) hindrance terms. It is linear in its six coefficients, so the code solves the normal equations directly.

$$\boxed{\log_{10}T_{1/2}=\frac{aZ+b}{\sqrt{Q_\alpha}}+(cZ+d)+h_Z(Z\bmod2)+h_N(N\bmod2)}$$
Parameters: \(Z\) = parent proton number; \(N\) = parent neutron number; \(Q_\alpha\) = alpha-decay energy; \(a,b,c,d\) = fitted coefficients for the smooth \(Z\)- and \(Q\)-dependence; \(h_Z\) = additional odd-proton hindrance coefficient; \(h_N\) = additional odd-neutron hindrance coefficient. \(Z\bmod2\) and \(N\bmod2\) are 1 for odd and 0 for even. Meaning: the hindrance terms allow odd-\(Z\) and odd-\(N\) nuclei to have systematically different half-lives.

04Automatic empirical-variable search

The Universal Fit section searches candidate predictors and fits linear combinations of them. Candidate models are compared using information criteria, residual metrics, cross-validation, correlation analysis, and Bayesian single-predictor regression.

$$\boxed{\log_{10}T_{1/2}=b+\sum_j a_jX_j}$$
CandidateImplemented variablePhysical/systematic role
\(Q^{-1/2}\)\(1/\sqrt{Q_\alpha}\)Basic Geiger–Nuttall predictor
\(ZQ^{-1/2}\)\(Z/\sqrt{Q_\alpha}\)Coulomb-weighted predictor
\(A^{1/3}Q^{-1/2}\)\(\sqrt[3]{A}/\sqrt{Q_\alpha}\)Size-weighted predictor
\(ZZ_d/\sqrt Q\)\(Z(Z-2)/\sqrt{Q_\alpha}\)Parent–daughter Coulomb predictor
\(\chi\)\(ZZ_d\sqrt{\tilde A/Q_\alpha}\)UDL-style Coulomb/kinematic variable
\(\rho\)\(\sqrt{\tilde A ZZ_d(A_1^{1/3}+A_2^{1/3})}\)UDL-style geometry variable
Other\(Q,Q^2,A,N-Z,Z_d/\sqrt Q,Z^2/\sqrt Q,\log_{10}Q\)Alternative and structural predictors

05Mass, binding and shell diagnostics

The Mass & Binding tab reconstructs experimental binding energy from atomic mass excesses and compares it with a semi-empirical mass formula. The displayed shell quantity is explicitly the empirical residual, not a microscopic Strutinsky correction.

$$B_{\rm exp}=Z\Delta_H+N\Delta_n-\mathrm{ME},\qquad B_{\rm shell}=B_{\rm exp}-B_{\rm SEMF}.$$ $$B_{\rm SEMF}=a_vA-a_sA^{2/3}-a_c\frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{1/3}}-a_a\frac{(A-2Z)^2}{A}+\delta.$$
Parameters: \(B_{\rm exp}\) = experimental binding energy; \(B_{\rm SEMF}\) = semi-empirical mass-formula binding energy; \(a_v,a_s,a_c,a_a\) = volume, surface, Coulomb and asymmetry coefficients; \(A\) = mass number; \(Z\) = proton number; \(N=A-Z\); \(\delta\) = pairing-energy term. Meaning: \(B_{\rm shell}=B_{\rm exp}-B_{\rm SEMF}\) is the residual binding not explained by the SEMF terms and is used here as an empirical shell diagnostic.

06Separation energies and stability

The drip-line and shell diagnostics use separation-energy behavior and the mass residual to identify changes in nuclear binding systematics.

$$S_n(A,Z)=M(A-1,Z)+m_n-M(A,Z),\qquad S_p(A,Z)=M(A-1,Z-1)+m_H-M(A,Z).$$
Parameters: \(S_n\) = neutron separation energy; \(S_p\) = proton separation energy; \(M(A,Z)\) = mass of the nucleus; \(m_n\) = neutron mass; \(m_H\) = hydrogen-atom mass. Meaning: positive separation energy indicates that removing the corresponding nucleon costs energy. Values approaching zero or becoming negative indicate proximity to, or crossing of, a drip-line region.

07Decay-WKB effective potential and all components

The WKB module uses the following explicit potential components. \(V_N(r)\) is built from any combination of the five nuclear-potential shapes checked in the left panel (summed together); each checked shape has its own independent \(V_0\), ro and a. The surface and spin-orbit terms are switched on with independent toggles and have their own parameters. All energies are in MeV and radii in fm. Colors below match the Potentials plot on the Decay-WKB tab: V_N teal, V_S violet, V_C amber, V_L rose, V_{SO} proton-color, V_eff cyan.

\(V_{\rm eff}(r)\) = \(V_N(r)\) + \(V_S(r)\) + \(V_C(r)\) + \(V_L(r)\) + \(V_{SO}(r)\),   
$$V_S(r)=4V_D\,f_s(r)\big[1-f_s(r)\big],\qquad f_s(r)=\frac{1}{1+e^{(r-R_S)/a_S}}, $$
$$V_C(r)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k_e Z_pZ_d}{2R_{\rm coul}}\left(3-\dfrac{r^2}{R_{\rm coul}^2}\right),&r\le R_{\rm coul},\\[4pt]\dfrac{k_e Z_pZ_d}{r},&r>R_{\rm coul},\end{cases}\qquad R_{\rm coul}=r_c A_{(\cdot)}^{1/3}.$$
$$V_L(r)=\frac{(\hbar c)^2(l+1/2)^2}{2\mu c^2r^2}.$$
$$V_{SO}(r)=V_{so}\,\frac{f'_s(r)}{r}\,\langle l\!\cdot\!s\rangle,\qquad f_s(r)=\frac{1}{1+e^{(r-R_{so})/a_{so}}},\qquad f'_s(r)=-\frac{1}{a_{so}}f_s(r)\big[1-f_s(r)\big].$$
ComponentEquation / implementationParameters used by the explorer
Woods–Saxon\(V_{N,i}(r)=\dfrac{-V_{0,i}}{1+e^{(r-R_i)/a_i}}\)Each shape \(i\) has its own \(V_{0,i}\), \({\rm ro}_i\) and \(a_i\) (defaults 180 MeV, 1.17 fm, 0.63 fm); \(R_i={\rm ro}_i A_d^{1/3}\) by default, or \({\rm ro}_i(A_p^{1/3}+A_d^{1/3})\). Any subset of the five shapes at left may be checked; their \(V_N\) contributions are summed.
WS squared\(V_{N,i}(r)=\dfrac{-V_{0,i}}{\left(1+e^{(r-R_i)/a_i}\right)^2}\)
Gaussian\(V_{N,i}(r)=-V_{0,i}\,e^{-\left[(r-R_i)/a_i\right]^2}\)
Yukawa\(V_{N,i}(r)=\dfrac{-V_{0,i}\,e^{-(r-R_i)/a_i}}{r}\)
Exponential\(V_{N,i}(r)=-V_{0,i}\,e^{-(r-R_i)/a_i}\)
Derivative / surface\(V_S(r)=4V_D\,f_s(r)\big[1-f_s(r)\big]\), with \(f_s(r)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{(r-R_S)/a_S}}\)
Equivalently \(V_S(r)=-4a_SV_Df_s'(r)\) — i.e. (minus) the radial derivative of a Woods–Saxon well. Because a bell-shaped function's derivative is peaked where the function changes fastest, \(V_S\) is largest right at the nuclear surface \(r\approx R_S\) and small both deep inside and far outside the nucleus, adding extra attraction localized to the surface region.		\(V_D=15\) MeV, its own surface ro (default 1.17 fm, giving \(R_S={\rm ro}_SA^{1/3}_{(\cdot)}\)) and \(a_S=0.63\) fm (labeled Surface as). Active when Add surface (derivative) term is checked.
Coulomb\(V_C(r)=\dfrac{k_eZ_pZ_d}{2R_{\rm coul}}\left(3-\dfrac{r^2}{R_{\rm coul}^2}\right)\) for \(r\le R_{\rm coul}\);
\(V_C(r)=\dfrac{k_eZ_pZ_d}{r}\) for \(r> R_{\rm coul}\)		Coulomb \(r_c=1.20\) fm; \(R_{\rm coul}=r_cA_d^{1/3}\) or \(r_c(A_p^{1/3}+A_d^{1/3})\) — same Radius convention selector as the nuclear shapes above; \(k_e=1.439964\) MeV·fm (implementation constant).
Centrifugal\(V_L=(\hbar c)^2(l+1/2)^2/(2\mu c^2r^2)\)\(l\) is manual or automatic from spin/parity; the \(l+1/2\) factor is the Langer correction; \(\mu\) is the channel reduced mass.
Spin-orbit\(V_{SO}(r)=V_{so}f'_s(r)\langle l\!\cdot\!s\rangle/r\), with \(f'_s(r)=-f_s(1-f_s)/a_{so}\)Independent toggle; \(V_{so}\) defaults to 6 MeV, \(R_{so}\) uses the Woods–Saxon radius, \(a_{so}\) uses the Woods–Saxon diffuseness, and \(\langle l\!\cdot\!s\rangle\) is entered manually. It is zero when the toggle is off or the factor is zero.
Total\(V_{\rm eff}=V_N+V_S+V_C+V_L+V_{SO}\)Turning points solve \(V_{\rm eff}(r)=Q\).
Important: the Yukawa and exponential shapes are evaluated exactly as \(-V_0e^{-(r-R)/a}\)-type forms (they can grow large as \(r\to0\), since \((r-R)/a<0\) there); this matches the literal forms selectable in the explorer rather than a regularized short-range Yukawa. The surface and spin-orbit terms are independent toggles, not tied to which nuclear shape(s) are active. The displayed default values are the current WKB control values in the explorer.
Optional extra \(V_N(r)\) terms: two further contributions can be added on top of the checked shapes, both summed directly into \(V_N(r)\) before \(V_S,V_C,V_L,V_{SO}\) are added. Custom analytical \(V_N(r)\): a user-typed algebraic expression in \(r\) (plus the symbols \(R,V_0,{\rm ro},a,A_p,A_d,Z_p,Z_d\) and \(\exp,\sqrt{\ },|\cdot|,\log,\sin,\cos,\pi,e\)), evaluated with the reference shape's \(V_0,{\rm ro},a\) (the checked Woods–Saxon shape, or the first checked shape if WS is off). Numerical \(V_N(r)\) table: a pasted list of \((r,V)\) pairs in fm/MeV, linearly interpolated between points and taken as \(0\) outside the tabulated range. Both are switched on with their own independent toggles in the Nuclear Potential panel and are reflected explicitly, with your entered values, in the equation table below the potential plot on the Decay-WKB tab.

08Turning points, barrier action and half-life

A physical WKB calculation requires three ordered turning points \(r_1<r_2<r_3\). Roots are located by radial scanning and refined with bisection. Simpson quadrature is then used for the action and allowed-region integrals.

$$G=\int_{r_2}^{r_3}\frac{\sqrt{2\mu[V_{\rm eff}(r)-Q]}}{\hbar}\,dr,$$ $$I_{BS}=\int_{r_1}^{r_2}k(r)\,dr,\qquad T_{\rm osc}=2\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\frac{dr}{v(r)},\quad\nu=T_{\rm osc}^{-1},$$ $$\boxed{T_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{P_\alpha\,\nu\,e^{-2G}}}.$$
Parameters: \(G\) = dimensionless barrier action; \(r_1,r_2,r_3\) = ordered turning points; \(Q\) = decay energy; \(\mu\) = reduced mass; \(\hbar\) = reduced Planck constant; \(P_{\alpha}\) = alpha preformation probability (0–1); \(\nu\) = assault frequency; \(k(r)\) = wave number in the classically allowed region; \(v(r)\) = radial velocity. Meaning: larger \(G\) gives stronger tunnelling suppression and a longer half-life; larger \(P_{\alpha}\) or \(\nu\) increases the decay rate.

Bohr–Sommerfeld quantization and the Wildermuth condition

The classically allowed pocket between \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) is quantized with the radial Bohr–Sommerfeld condition. The wave number used by the explorer is \(k(r)=\sqrt{2\mu[Q-V_{\rm eff}(r)]}/\hbar\) wherever \(Q>V_{\rm eff}(r)\).

$$\boxed{I_{BS}=\int_{r_1}^{r_2}k(r)\,dr=\left(n+\frac12\right)\pi},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots$$ $$\boxed{G_W=2n+l=\sum_i g_i},\qquad \boxed{n_W=\frac{G_W-l}{2}}.$$
How a user applies Wildermuth: first determine the emitted cluster orbital angular momentum \(l\). Then assign each cluster nucleon to its oscillator major shell in the daughter-plus-cluster configuration and sum the corresponding oscillator quanta \(g_i=2n_i+l_i\). This sum is the Wildermuth number \(G_W\). The radial node number to test in the Bohr–Sommerfeld condition is \(n_W=(G_W-l)/2\). A valid assignment should give a non-negative integer \(n_W\); if it does not, revisit the shell assignment or the chosen \(l\).
Numerical check: after calculating \(I_{BS}\), compare it with \((n_W+1/2)\pi\). The mismatch is \(\Delta_{BS}=I_{BS}-(n_W+1/2)\pi\); values near zero indicate that the selected potential and Q value support the chosen Wildermuth quantum number. For the displayed automatic estimate, the code uses \(n_{\rm best}=\max\{0,\operatorname{round}[I_{BS}/\pi-1/2]\}\).
Implementation note. In the current code, the Bohr–Sommerfeld quantization condition is not used in the actual WKB calculation: we do not solve the potential from BS, nor do we enforce BS when computing the barrier action \(G\), assault frequency or half-life. The Bohr–Sommerfeld integral \(I_{BS}\), the displayed \(n\)(best), and the residual are only diagnostic checks for the chosen potential and radial quantum number. In principle, BS can be used to eliminate one free parameter of the potential, but that is not implemented here. The same applies to the p/2p tab, where the displayed BS n is not used to modify the WKB result.

09Angular momentum and branching

For alpha decay, the automatic-\(l\) option uses parsed spin/parity information to select the lowest angular momentum compatible with the spin difference and parity conservation.

$$|J_i-J_f|\le l\le J_i+J_f,\qquad \pi_i=\pi_f(-1)^l.$$
Parameters: \(J_i,J_f\) = initial and final nuclear spins; \(\pi_i,\pi_f\) = initial and final parities; \(l\) = orbital angular momentum carried by the emitted cluster. Meaning: the first relation gives the allowed angular-momentum range, while the parity relation determines whether \(l\) must be even or odd. Higher \(l\) adds centrifugal-barrier suppression.

10Fit statistics and optimization

Every empirical regression in the explorer (Geiger–Nuttall, Viola–Seaborg, Universal/Automatic-variable fit, β/Cluster Universal Fit) is scored with the same log-space statistics, computed from the fitted model evaluated at each data point. Throughout, \(y=\log_{10}T_{1/2}\) is the fitted response.

Experimental value

\(y_i^{\rm exp}=\log_{10}T_{1/2,i}^{\rm exp}\)
\(y_i^{\rm exp}\) = the measured (NUBASE2020-tabulated) half-life of data point \(i\), converted to \(\log_{10}\) (seconds), because half-lives span many orders of magnitude and the regression is performed in log space rather than on \(T_{1/2}\) directly. \(T_{1/2,i}^{\rm exp}\) = the tabulated experimental half-life of nuclide/point \(i\). \(i\) = index running over the \(N\) data points in the currently filtered dataset.

Model value

\(y_i^{\rm model}=\hat f(x_i;\,\hat\theta)\)
\(y_i^{\rm model}\) = the fitted model's prediction of \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\) for point \(i\), obtained by evaluating the regression formula for the fit family in use (Geiger–Nuttall, Viola–Seaborg, or the linear combination \(b+\sum_ja_jX_j\) from card 04) with the fitted coefficients. \(\hat f(\cdot)\) = the model function for that fit family. \(x_i\) = the predictor value(s) for point \(i\) (e.g. \(Q_\alpha\), \(Z\), or the chosen candidate variables \(X_j\)). \(\hat\theta\) = the fitted coefficient vector (e.g. \(a,b\) for Geiger–Nuttall, or \(a,b,c,d,h_Z,h_N\) for Viola–Seaborg) obtained by least squares.

Residual \(\Delta_i\)

\(\Delta_i=y_i^{\rm model}-y_i^{\rm exp}\)
\(\Delta_i\) = the signed residual (error) of the fit at point \(i\), in units of \(\log_{10}\)(seconds) since \(y=\log_{10}T_{1/2}\). Sign: \(\Delta_i>0\) means the model over-predicts the half-life (longer than observed); \(\Delta_i<0\) means it under-predicts it (shorter than observed). Magnitude: because \(y\) is a base-10 log, \(\Delta_i=+1\) means the model's half-life is \(10\times\) too long, and \(\Delta_i=-1\) means \(10\times\) too short — smaller \(|\Delta_i|\) is a better point-by-point fit.

\(N\)

\(N=\) count of fitted data points
\(N\) = the number of nuclides/channels in the current filtered dataset (species selection, \(Z\)/\(A\) range, decay-mode and branching-ratio cuts) that have finite, usable predictor and response values, i.e. the number of points actually entering the regression. Larger \(N\) gives more stable coefficient estimates and a more reliable RMSE/AIC/BIC comparison between candidate models.

\(k\)

\(k=p=\) number of fitted parameters
\(k\) (also denoted \(p\) in the implementation) = the number of free coefficients estimated by least squares for that model, i.e. the length of \(\hat\theta\). Examples: \(k=2\) for Geiger–Nuttall (\(a,b\)); \(k=6\) for the full Viola–Seaborg-type relation (\(a,b,c,d,h_Z,h_N\)); \(k=1+(\text{number of selected candidate terms})\) for the Universal/Automatic-variable fit (the \(+1\) is the intercept \(b\)). \(k\) is the "complexity" that the degrees of freedom and AIC/BIC below penalize against.

Degrees of freedom

\(\mathrm{dof}=N-k\)
\(\mathrm{dof}\) = the number of data points in excess of what is needed to determine the \(k\) fitted parameters exactly, using \(N\) and \(k\) as defined above. A fit with \(\mathrm{dof}\le0\) is under- or exactly-determined (no genuine residual information remains to judge goodness of fit); the explorer reports \(\mathrm{dof}=\max(N-k,0)\) and treats the reduced-\(\chi^2\) below as undefined (\(\mathrm{NaN}\)) when \(\mathrm{dof}\le0\).

RMSE

\(\displaystyle{\rm RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\Delta_i^2}\)
RMSE = root-mean-square error, the typical (quadratic-mean) size of the residual in \(\log_{10}(T_{1/2})\) units, built from \(\Delta_i\) and \(N\) above. Because large residuals are squared before averaging, RMSE penalizes big outlier errors more heavily than MAE; it is reported for every regression and used as the default sort/ranking metric in several tables.

MAE

\(\displaystyle{\rm MAE}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N|\Delta_i|\)
MAE = mean absolute error, the average magnitude of the residual regardless of sign, in the same \(\log_{10}(T_{1/2})\) units as \(\Delta_i\). Unlike RMSE it weights every point linearly, so it is less sensitive to a few large outliers and gives a more "typical-case" sense of fit quality.

\(\chi^2\) (sum of squares)

\(\displaystyle\chi^2\equiv{\rm SS}=\sum_{i=1}^N\Delta_i^2\)
\(\chi^2\) (labelled SS, the residual sum of squares, in the fit-routine code) = the unweighted sum of squared residuals over all \(N\) points. Because the empirical fits carry no per-point experimental uncertainty \(\sigma_i\) in this explorer, this is an unweighted \(\sum\Delta_i^2\) rather than the usual \(\sum(\Delta_i/\sigma_i)^2\); it is the quantity minimized by the ordinary-least-squares solve and is the direct input to RMSE, the reduced \(\chi^2\), AIC and BIC below.

Reduced \(\chi^2\)

\(\displaystyle\chi^2_\nu=\frac{\chi^2}{N-k}=\frac{\rm SS}{\mathrm{dof}}\)
\(\chi^2_\nu\) = the residual sum of squares divided by the degrees of freedom, i.e. the mean squared residual after accounting for the \(k\) fitted parameters, using \(\chi^2\), \(N\), \(k\), \(\mathrm{dof}=N-k\) as above. It rescales the raw \(\chi^2\) so fits with different numbers of data points or parameters can be compared on the same footing; the explorer returns it as undefined (\(\mathrm{NaN}\)) when \(\mathrm{dof}\le0\).

AIC

\(\displaystyle{\rm AIC}=N\ln\!\left(\frac{\rm SS}{N}\right)+2k\)
AIC = Akaike Information Criterion, exactly as implemented in the fit code. \({\rm SS}=\chi^2\) = residual sum of squares; \(N\) = number of data points; \(k\) = number of fitted parameters, with \(2k\) the complexity penalty (twice the parameter count). The first term \(N\ln({\rm SS}/N)\) shrinks as the fit gets tighter, while \(2k\) grows with model complexity; lower AIC is better, and it is used to compare non-nested models of different complexity while discouraging over-fitting with extra free parameters.

BIC

\(\displaystyle{\rm BIC}=N\ln\!\left(\frac{\rm SS}{N}\right)+k\ln N\)
BIC = Bayesian Information Criterion, exactly as implemented in the fit code, using the same SS, N, k as AIC, but with complexity penalty \(k\ln N\) instead of \(2k\). Because \(\ln N>2\) whenever \(N>7\), BIC penalizes extra parameters more heavily than AIC for typical dataset sizes here, so it favors sparser models more strongly as \(N\) grows; lower BIC is better, and it is offered alongside AIC as an alternative ranking metric with a stronger preference for simplicity.

CV RMSE

\(\displaystyle{\rm CV\,RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\big(y_i-\hat f_{-{\rm fold}(i)}(x_i)\big)^2}\)
CV RMSE = \(k\)-fold cross-validated RMSE. The dataset is split into the selected number of folds; for each fold the model is refit on the remaining folds and evaluated on the held-out points, and the squared held-out errors are pooled over all \(N\) points before taking the square root. \(\hat f_{-{\rm fold}(i)}\) = the model refit without the fold containing point \(i\). Because it is evaluated on data not used to fit the corresponding coefficients, CV RMSE is a more robust indicator of out-of-sample predictive accuracy than the in-sample RMSE above, and is used for comparing candidate models in the Universal/Automatic-variable and β/Cluster fits.

The global WKB optimizer performs a reproducible, bounded search over the selected model family and parameter space. It evaluates every permitted potential combination, keeps the lowest-error parameter set for each combination, and ranks the combinations by the selected objective. The search uses the full filtered dataset, while the final batch report reuses the exact applied global result so that GLOBAL ANALYSIS and BATCH PERFORMANCE report identical statistics. Batch results are sorted systematically before the train/test split.

Global optimization. “Search evaluations per combination” is the number of trial parameter sets tested for one potential combination. Increasing it improves the chance of finding a lower minimum but increases runtime. The global winner is not applied automatically: press Apply best combination, then run the batch again to evaluate that applied model.

What does Δ mean? Delta (\(\Delta\)) is simply the difference between prediction and experiment: \(\Delta=\log_{10}T_{\rm model}-\log_{10}T_{\rm exp}\). For example, \(\Delta=+1\) means the model predicts a half-life 10 times longer than experiment; \(\Delta=-1\) means 10 times shorter. Thus smaller \(|\Delta|\) is better.
Interpretation. The empirical models describe fitted NUBASE2020 systematics; the WKB result additionally depends on the selected potential, angular momentum, numerical settings, and preformation probability.

12Proton and two-proton decay

The p and 2p tab applies the same three-turning-point WKB machinery to a one-proton or two-proton emitter, while keeping the channel-specific mass, charge, Q-value and angular-momentum inputs explicit.

$$Q_p=M(A,Z)-M(A-1,Z-1)-M(^1\!H),$$ $$Q_{2p}=M(A,Z)-M(A-2,Z-2)-2M(^1\!H).$$
Q-value source: proton emission uses the embedded NUBASE2020 database field \(Q_p\). For 2p emission, a dedicated \(Q_{2p}\) field is preferred when available; otherwise the value is calculated from the embedded mass excesses and marked as calculated from database masses. A calculated positive Q value is an energetic channel, not evidence that an experimental 2p decay has been observed.
$$\mu=\frac{m_pm_d}{m_p+m_d},\qquad V_{\rm eff}(r)=V_N(r)+V_S(r)+V_{SO}(r)+V_C(r)+V_L(r),$$ $$V_L(r)=\frac{(\hbar c)^2(L_{\rm eff}+1/2)^2}{2\mu c^2r^2},\qquad L_{\rm eff}=\begin{cases}l,&p\\L_{\rm trial},&2p.\end{cases}$$
Reduced mass: \(m_p\) denotes the emitted cluster mass, not the parent-nucleus mass. In the implementation, p emission uses the mass of one hydrogen atom and 2p emission uses twice that mass: mp = wkbMass(^1H) or mp = 2*wkbMass(^1H). This \(m_p\) is used directly in \(\mu=m_pm_d/(m_p+m_d)\), the centrifugal potential and the WKB integrals. The parent and daughter masses are otherwise obtained separately from the embedded mass data.
Angular momentum: for p emission, \(l\) is the single-proton orbital angular momentum. For 2p emission, \(L\) is the total two-proton orbital angular momentum and the trial effective \(L\) is used by the barrier calculation. The code derives candidate values from parent/daughter \(J^\pi\) only when the assignment is unique; it does not invent an experimental \(L\).
$$\pi_i=\pi_f(-1)^l,\qquad |J_f-j_p|\le J_i\le J_f+j_p,$$ $$j_p=\begin{cases}\tfrac12,&l=0\\l-\tfrac12\ \text{or}\ l+\tfrac12,&l>0.\end{cases}$$
How Derived L is obtained: the channel builder parses the parent and daughter spin/parity values as \(J_i^{\pi_i}\) and \(J_f^{\pi_f}\). It tests integer \(l\) values from 0 through 12. A candidate is retained only when parity is conserved, \(\pi_i=\pi_f(-1)^l\), and at least one emitted-proton angular momentum \(j_p\) satisfies the triangle condition above. For \(l=0\), the only candidate is \(j_p=1/2\); for \(l>0\), both \(j_p=l-1/2\) and \(j_p=l+1/2\) are tested. Duplicate \(l\) values are removed and sorted. The result is displayed as Derived L only when exactly one \(l\) remains; otherwise it is shown as not uniquely derived.
2p interpretation: the current implementation uses this same parsed-\(J^\pi\), parity and single-proton-coupling candidate search for the 2p channel. A unique candidate can populate the effective 2p \(L\) when Use derived L when unique is enabled; otherwise the user supplies the trial effective \(L\). This is an effective exploratory prescription, not a full three-body treatment of proton-proton angular-momentum coupling.
Quantityp emission2p emission
Emitted clusterone proton, \(A_e=1, Z_e=1\)two-proton cluster, \(A_e=2, Z_e=2\)
Daughter\((A-1,Z-1)\)\((A-2,Z-2)\)
Coulomb charge\(Z_eZ_d=Z_d\)\(Z_eZ_d=2Z_d\)
Preformation input\(P_p\)\(P_{2p}\)
Experimental comparisonUses available proton half-life and branching dataOnly uses experimental half-life when present; otherwise the residual is unavailable
Interpretation. The p and 2p results are model calculations. They depend on the selected nuclear-potential terms, radius convention, Coulomb radius, angular momentum, preformation probability, radial grid and root tolerance. A valid result requires three ordered turning points \(r_1<r_2<r_3\); otherwise the channel is reported as invalid.

13Neutron and two-neutron decay

The n and 2n tab applies the same three-turning-point WKB barrier procedure to neutral emission. It is a one-dimensional effective-barrier model: it does not solve the microscopic nuclear interaction, neutron pairing dynamics, or a full three-body 2n decay problem.

$$Q_n=\big[M(A,Z)-M(A-1,Z)-m_n\big]c^2,$$ $$V_{\rm eff}(r)=V_N(r)+V_S(r)+V_{SO}(r)+V_L(r),\qquad V_C(r)=0,$$ $$V_L(r)=\frac{(\hbar c)^2(L_{\rm eff}+1/2)^2}{2\mu c^2r^2}.$$
Q-value and data source: for neutron emission, the channel builder uses the embedded NUBASE2020 Qn field, converted from keV to MeV, and the daughter is \((A-1,Z)\). For the current 2n option, the daughter is \((A-2,Z)\) and the implementation uses the available embedded Qn value as a documented two-neutron proxy; it is labeled “embedded Qn / 2n proxy” rather than presented as a dedicated experimental Q2n. A positive Q establishes energetic allowance, not an observed decay branch.
Neutral-particle barrier: because the emitted neutron or neutron pair has zero charge, there is no Coulomb term. The barrier is supplied by the nuclear terms, optional surface and spin-orbit terms, and the centrifugal term. The selected radius convention still controls the nuclear-shape radii.
$$\pi_i=\pi_f(-1)^l,\qquad |J_f-j_n|\le J_i\le J_f+j_n,$$ $$j_n=\begin{cases}\tfrac12,&l=0\\l-\tfrac12\ \text{or}\ l+\tfrac12,&l>0.\end{cases}$$
Derived L: the channel builder parses parent and daughter Jπ values, accepts standard forms such as \(1/2(+)\) and \((3/2)^-\), tests integer neutron orbital values \(l=0,\ldots,12\), enforces parity conservation and the spin triangle condition, removes duplicates, and displays a value only when exactly one candidate remains. For an s-wave neutron, \(l=0\) couples to neutron spin \(1/2\); it is not treated as \(j_n=0\). If the input spins are missing or the assignment is ambiguous, the audit correctly reports “undetermined”.
2n angular momentum: the current 2n calculation uses the same effective candidate search and trial \(L\) controls as the exploratory barrier model. When Use derived L when unique is enabled, a unique candidate can seed the effective barrier; otherwise the user-controlled \(L\), \(L_{\rm eff}\), and fallback trial values are used. This is not a microscopic coupling calculation for two correlated neutrons.
Audit and batch results: the database audit lists parent, daughter, decay type, Q value, tabulated half-life, derived L, Jπ values, branching information, and data status. The WKB-versus-experiment and residual plots include only channels with usable experimental half-lives. The batch table may contain valid calculated channels whose experimental half-life or branching information is unavailable.
Optimization: the n/2n optimizer minimizes RMSE in \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\) over the currently filtered channels with finite experimental half-lives. It searches the active nuclear-shape parameters and preformation factor with the selected bounded method, applies the best result, then recalculates the selected channel and batch. Increase evaluations for a more thorough search and compare the optimized result with the unoptimized baseline.
Interpretation. The n and 2n outputs are effective WKB estimates. A valid result requires three ordered turning points \(r_1<r_2<r_3\); otherwise the channel is rejected at the current parameter values. The calculation is not a full weak-interaction, pairing, or three-body decay solver.

14Spontaneous-fission systematics

The Spontaneous Fission tab analyzes nuclides with an explicit SF branching ratio and fits the SF partial half-life, rather than the total half-life, so competing alpha or beta branches are not interpreted as fission.

$$T_{\rm SF}=\frac{T_{1/2}}{BR_{\rm SF}/100},\qquad y_{\rm SF}=\log_{10}T_{\rm SF}.$$
Data selection: only explicit SF / spontaneous fission branch keys are used. The tab supports a Z range, an optional Dominant SF branch only filter, a minimum SF branching-ratio threshold, and three selectable empirical models. The fitted response is in log10 seconds.
$$\boxed{x=\frac{Z^2}{50.883\,A\left[1-1.7826\left(\frac{N-Z}{A}\right)^2\right]}}$$ $$\boxed{\log_{10}T_{\rm SF}=a+bx+cx^2+h_Z(Z\bmod2)+h_N(N\bmod2)}$$
Fissility variable: \(x\) is the liquid-drop/Swiatecki-style fissility coordinate used by the explorer. \(A\) is mass number, \(Z\) proton number and \(N=A-Z\). The denominator contains an asymmetry correction through \((N-Z)^2/A^2\). Larger fissility generally corresponds to a stronger tendency toward fission, but the fitted relation is empirical and does not itself calculate a microscopic fission barrier.
ModelImplemented relationFree parameters
Linear fissility\(\log_{10}T_{\rm SF}=a+bx\)\(a,b\) (k=2)
Quadratic fissility\(\log_{10}T_{\rm SF}=a+bx+cx^2\)\(a,b,c\) (k=3)
Quadratic + odd-even hindrance\(\log_{10}T_{\rm SF}=a+bx+cx^2+h_Z(Z\bmod2)+h_N(N\bmod2)\)\(a,b,c,h_Z,h_N\) (k=5)
Fit parameters: \(a\) is the intercept; \(b\) is the linear fissility coefficient; \(c\) is the quadratic curvature coefficient; \(h_Z\) is the odd-Z hindrance offset; and \(h_N\) is the odd-N hindrance offset. The selected model's fitted values are displayed directly in MODEL → FIT PARAMETERS.
Residual: \(\Delta=\log_{10}T_{\rm SF,model}-\log_{10}T_{\rm SF,exp}\). Positive \(\Delta\) means the model predicts a longer SF partial half-life; negative \(\Delta\) means a shorter one. The residual plot is shown versus \(Z\).
Model comparison: the Multi-Model Comparison panel fits all three systematics to the same filtered dataset and reports \(k\), \(N\), RMSE, MAE, \(R^2\), SSE/(N-k), AIC and BIC. Models are ranked by RMSE. Because the embedded SF records do not provide per-point experimental uncertainties for this regression, SSE/(N-k) is an unweighted residual-variance diagnostic, not a formal uncertainty-weighted reduced \(\chi^2\).
Scope and interpretation. The SF model is a descriptive systematics regression. It does not compute a microscopic fission barrier, collective inertia, multidimensional tunnelling path, or fragment mass distribution. Its extrapolation outside the fitted fissility/Z region should therefore be treated cautiously.

15Decay-chain / Bateman systematics

The Decay Chain tab follows a radioactive parent through its supported daughter network using the embedded NUBASE decay modes and branching fractions. It solves the coupled Bateman population equations in time and reports both nuclide abundances and activities.

\[\frac{dN_i}{dt}=-\lambda_iN_i+\sum_j b_{j\to i}\lambda_jN_j\] \[\lambda_i=\frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2,i}},\qquad A_i(t)=\lambda_iN_i(t)\]
Network construction: the parent is the initial population. Supported daughter-producing branches are followed recursively; branching fractions determine the transfer of population between connected nuclides. Spontaneous fission is excluded from the unique-daughter Bateman network because a fission branch requires fragment-yield information rather than one uniquely defined daughter.
Stable endpoints: stable daughters have \(\lambda=0\) and therefore accumulate as terminal populations. The network table identifies the nuclides, half-lives, decay constants, branches and endpoints used in the calculation.
Abundance: \(N_i(t)\) is the population of nuclide \(i\). The abundance plot can show absolute populations or populations normalized to the initial parent population \(N_0\). Activities are \(A_i=\lambda_iN_i\) and are therefore zero for stable endpoints.
Decay-chain diagram: the pathway diagram displays the same network used by the simulator, including decay modes and branching percentages. Reconverging pathways may be displayed explicitly so that alternative routes remain visible.
Interpretation. This is a deterministic linear decay-network calculation based on the embedded half-lives and branching data. It is not a full nuclear-reaction or fission-fragment transport model. Results are only as complete as the supported decay branches and daughter information in the dataset.
User guide · NUBASE2020 Decay Systematics Explorer

Manual and recommended workflow

Use the tabs as complementary views of the same embedded nuclear dataset. The steps below describe the controls and the order that is most useful for a quantitative alpha-decay study.

01Quick start

1

Decay Systematics

Choose a preset or configure decay mode, axes, Z range, branching threshold, and plotting options. Click a table row to inspect a nuclide.

2

Mass & Binding

Inspect experimental binding energy, SEMF binding, pairing, shell residuals, and separation energies.

3

Drip-Line & Shell

Use separation-energy and shell-residual views to identify local stability and shell effects.

4

Empirical α Decay

Filter alpha emitters and compare Geiger–Nuttall and Viola–Seaborg fits with residual diagnostics and the automatic predictor search.

5

β / Cluster Universal Fit

Select a family, candidate terms, maximum number of terms, CV folds, and ranking metric. Inspect the best model and correlation/Bayesian diagnostics.

6

Decay-WKB

Start with one channel, inspect the potential and turning points, then run the global optimization and record the winning combination, parameter values, objective, and evaluation count. Apply the winner before running the selected-family batch.

7

p and 2p DECAY

Analyze proton emission or two-proton candidates from the embedded NUBASE2020 records. Qp is taken from the database; Q₂p is used directly only if a dedicated field exists, otherwise it is calculated from the embedded masses and labeled accordingly. Experimental L is never invented.

8

n and 2n DECAY

Analyze neutron or two-neutron candidates using the embedded Qn data, neutral-particle effective barrier, derived-L audit, batch residuals and bounded potential optimization. The 2n mode is explicitly a Qn-based proxy in the current implementation.

02p and 2p workflow

A

Select the emitter family

Choose Proton emission or Two-proton emission first. The channel list, daughter nucleus, Q source, Coulomb charge and angular-momentum interpretation update with the family.

B

Verify the database audit

Check the parent, daughter, Q value, Q source, half-life, branching information and data status. For 2p entries, distinguish a mass-derived Q₂p from a dedicated experimental/database value.

C

Set the quantum inputs

For p emission, set single-proton l. For 2p emission, set total L and trial effective L. Enable Use derived L when unique only when the displayed Jπ values support a unique assignment; an unavailable or non-unique value remains a user-controlled trial.

D

Run one channel first

Keep the baseline Woods–Saxon term enabled, choose a radius convention, and press Calculate selected. Inspect the potential, Q line, three turning points, G, assault frequency, log₁₀ T and the experimental comparison before changing more parameters.

E

Run and interpret the batch

Apply Z/A and branch filters, choose branch correction and train fraction, then run the family batch. Compare train and test RMSE only for channels with usable experimental half-lives; mass-derived 2p candidates are not automatically experimental 2p observations.

F

Optimize last

After recording a baseline, optimize the selected potential and preformation settings. Save the objective, method, evaluation count, radius convention, angular-momentum inputs and filters with the result.

03Default WKB benchmark channel

The individual-channel drawer is initialized to the valid channel α + 106Te → 102Sn whenever that channel is present under the current alpha filters. This is the physically valid interpretation of the requested “α + 10Te → 102Sn” notation: adding an alpha particle to \(^{102}\mathrm{Sn}\) gives \(^{106}\mathrm{Te}\).

Why this matters. The embedded dataset contains \(^{106}\mathrm{Te}\) and \(^{102}\mathrm{Sn}\); the daughter \(^{102}\mathrm{Sn}\) therefore corresponds to the parent \(^{106}\mathrm{Te}\) for alpha emission.

04n and 2n workflow

A

Select the emitter family

Choose Neutron emission or Two-neutron emission. The daughter, Q value, source label, channel list and audit table update with the selection and current Z/A filters.

B

Read the database audit

Check Q, half-life, derived L, parent/daughter Jπ, branching information and status. For 2n entries, remember that the current Q source is an embedded Qn / 2n proxy, not a dedicated experimental Q2n measurement.

C

Set angular momentum

Keep Use derived L when unique enabled when reliable Jπ values are available. For neutron emission, l = 0 means s-wave emission with neutron spin j = 1/2. For ambiguous cases, inspect the candidate assignment and set l, total L or effective L manually.

D

Calculate one channel

Keep a nuclear shape enabled, choose the radius convention, press Calculate selected, and inspect the neutral effective potential, Q line, three turning points, action G, assault frequency and log10 half-life.

E

Run the batch

Filter by family, dominant mode, Z and A, then run the neutron batch. Interpret residual plots only for channels with finite experimental half-lives; valid barrier solutions can still lack experimental comparison data.

F

Optimize after the baseline

Record the baseline first. Choose a bounded optimization method and evaluation count, press Optimize Potential, then compare the reported RMSE and refreshed batch results with the baseline. The optimizer changes active shape parameters and preformation; it does not create experimental Q2n data.

04Recommended alpha/WKB workflow

A

Check the channel note

Confirm parent, daughter, Q value, and experimental \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\).

B

Inspect the potential

Verify the three turning points and the barrier region between \(r_2\) and \(r_3\). The table below the plot ("Effective potential — your parameter values") shows the exact numeric equation for each active term, so you can cross-check the plot against the formula being evaluated.

C

Check \(l\) and preformation

Keep Auto \(l\) enabled when reliable \(J^\pi\) values are available; record \(P_\alpha\) because it directly changes the predicted decay rate.

D

Read residuals

Use \(\Delta\log_{10}T=\log_{10}T_{\rm WKB}-\log_{10}T_{\rm exp}\) and the WKB-versus-experiment plot to diagnose systematic offsets.

E

Optimize last

Only after a baseline calculation should you optimize \(V_0,r_0,a,r_C\) and optionally \(P_\alpha\).

05Global optimization and batch validation

1

Choose the search scope

Set the emitter family, Z/A filters, potential-shape checkboxes, surface-term option, radius convention, and objective before starting Global Analysis. These settings define the combinations that are searched.

2

Set search evaluations

Use “Search evaluations per combination” to control how many parameter trials are tested for each candidate combination. Start with a moderate value for exploration, then increase it for the final search.

3

Compare the global results

Review the ranked combinations using RMSE, MAE, R², valid-count, and the selected objective. Prefer a physically sensible model with good error and adequate valid coverage, not only the smallest score.

4

Apply and validate

Press Apply best combination to copy the winning model and parameters into the WKB controls. Then press Run selected family. The batch report should reuse the applied global result and therefore match the global statistics exactly.

06WKB controls

ControlEffectRecommended use
Emitter familyAlpha or cluster familyKeep α for ordinary alpha-decay studies.
Individual channelDetailed single-channel calculationStart with α + 106Te → 102Sn.
Potential modelWS / WS² / Gaussian / Yukawa / Exponential (any combination, summed) + optional surface term, plus an optional custom analytical \(V_N(r)\) formula and/or an optional numerical \((r,V)\) table, both added into \(V_N(r)\)Use Woods–Saxon alone as the baseline; reach for the custom/numerical terms only for a specific literature potential.
Radius conventionDefines both the nuclear-shape radii \(R_i\) and the Coulomb radius \(R_{\rm coul}\) (same selector, applied consistently to both)Record the convention with every fit.
Auto \(l\)Uses spin/parity constraintsLeave ON when the quantum numbers are usable.
Branch correctionUses alpha partial half-life when possibleUseful for non-100% alpha branches.
rmax / drRadial numerical domain/resolutionSmaller \(dr\) gives finer integration at higher cost.
OptimizationSearches potential/preformation parametersCompare against an unoptimized baseline.

The panel below the potential plot ("Effective potential — your parameter values") writes out \(V_N,V_S,V_C,V_L\) and their sum with the currently selected numbers substituted in, so you can read off exactly what was calculated for the current channel without leaving the tab.

07Reading empirical model statistics

  • RMSE / MAE: lower is better in \(\log_{10}T_{1/2}\) space.
  • \(R^2\): measures fitted variance; it is not independent validation when evaluated on the same fitting sample.
  • Reduced \(\chi^2\): the empirical alpha implementation uses unweighted log residuals because per-nuclide experimental uncertainties are not part of the embedded alpha dataset.
  • AIC/BIC: penalize extra parameters and are useful when comparing models of different complexity.
  • CV RMSE: use this to assess candidate models beyond their in-sample fit.

08Common pitfalls

  • Changing the Z range changes the fitted empirical coefficients.
  • A positive Q value establishes energetic allowance, not a unique half-life.
  • A high in-sample \(R^2\) is not independent predictive validation.
  • A WKB case with fewer than three turning points is rejected by the implementation.
  • The shell plot is the empirical residual \(B_{\rm exp}-B_{\rm SEMF}\), not a microscopic Strutinsky calculation.
Best practice. Establish systematics with the empirical tab, inspect structure with Mass & Binding / Drip-Line & Shell, and then test a physical barrier picture with WKB.

09Spontaneous-fission workflow

A

Select the SF dataset

Open SPONTANEOUS FISSION and choose the Z range. The tab uses records with an explicit SF branching ratio. Check the DATA AUDIT before fitting.

B

Control the branch selection

Enable Dominant SF branch only when you want only nuclei whose listed dominant decay mode is fission. Use Minimum SF branching (%) to exclude weak SF branches. Remember that the fitted quantity is the SF partial half-life, \(T_{\rm SF}=T_{1/2}/(BR_{\rm SF}/100)\).

C

Choose the empirical model

Compare Linear fissility (2 parameters), Quadratic fissility (3 parameters), and Quadratic + odd-even hindrance (5 parameters). The last model adds separate odd-Z and odd-N offsets.

D

Read MODEL and FIT PARAMETERS

Inspect the fissility equation and the fitted coefficients \(a,b,c,h_Z,h_N\) that are actually used for the selected model. Record these values with the filter settings if the fit is used in a report.

E

Inspect residuals

Use the SF residual plot and RESIDUAL STATISTICS. \(\Delta=\log_{10}T_{\rm SF,model}-\log_{10}T_{\rm SF,exp}\); smaller absolute residuals are better. Look for systematic trends with Z or isolated outliers rather than relying on a single summary number.

F

Compare all models

Read MULTI-MODEL COMPARISON after the SF-branching table. RMSE and MAE measure prediction error; \(R^2\) describes in-sample variance explained; AIC and BIC penalize additional parameters. A lower score is preferred for each criterion, but model simplicity and physical plausibility should also be considered.

G

Do not over-interpret extrapolation

The SF fit is empirical. A good in-sample fit does not establish a microscopic fission mechanism or guarantee reliable predictions far outside the fitted Z/fissility region.

10Decay-chain / Bateman workflow

A

Select the parent

Open DECAY CHAIN and select a parent nuclide from the embedded dataset. The simulator builds the supported daughter network from the listed decay branches.

B

Run the Bateman simulation

Choose the time range and resolution as provided by the tab, then click Simulate chain. The coupled populations are evolved from the initial parent population.

C

Read the pathway diagram

Use the decay-chain diagram to identify daughter pathways, decay modes and branching percentages. Stable nuclides are shown as terminal endpoints.

D

Inspect abundance and activity

The Abundance vs time plot shows \(N_i(t)\); the optional Activity vs time plot shows \(A_i(t)=\lambda_iN_i(t)\). Normalized abundance/activity can be used to compare chains independent of the starting population.

E

Check the decay network table

Verify the half-life, \(\lambda\), branches and endpoint status for each network member. This table is the audit trail for the Bateman calculation.

F

Interpret branching correctly

Branching fractions redistribute population among supported daughters. A spontaneous-fission branch is not assigned a unique daughter because fragment yields are not represented in this Bateman network.

11Reproducibility checklist

For a report or publication, record the selected tab, Z/A ranges, dominant-branch and minimum-BR settings, empirical model/candidate terms, WKB potential convention, \(l\), \(P_\alpha\), \(r_{\max}\), \(dr\), and optimization settings. These controls can materially change the result.
